newsitem.title: GERMANY: New attempt set to solve German metal pay row.
newsitem.headline: New attempt set to solve German metal pay row.

text.p: German metal and engineering employers will meet union leaders in the steel-making region of North-Rhine Westphalia in a new bid to solve the pay row in the sector, the two sides said on Tuesday.

At the centre of the dispute is a new law cutting sick pay entitlement from the current 100 percent of worker salaries to 80 percent, which worker representatives say would be in breach of employee contracts in the sector.
The talks have been set for next Monday and are likely to take place in Duesseldorf, a spokesman at the headquarters of the Gesamtmetall employers federation said in response to a telephone enquiry.
The meeting had been scheduled to take place on Tuesday this week but was called off last Monday with no reason given by either side.

Harald Schartau, head of the regional branch of the IG Metall engineering trade union in North-Rhine Westphalia, was quoted in a newspaper report on Tuesday as saying there were "new ideas" on the issue that were worth exploring.
Nobody from the regional union leadership was immediately available to confirm what new options would be included in the discussions.
Negotiations on sick pay and other planned cuts to worker benefits have been thrown out to regional wage committees after a bid to solve the dispute at a national level failed last month.
Since then, a further attempt to find points of agreement between workers and employers on the issue have also failed in the south-west state of Baden-Wuerttemberg.

Metal and engineering employers argue that cuts to non-wage labour costs are essential to restore the competitivity of the industry, where it said firms overall will see a 10 percent decline in earnings this year.
North-Rhine Westphalia is home to some of Germany's largest steel producers and employs a large percentage of the some 3.5 million workers in the metal and engineering sector.

News of the new talks came as the head of Germany's Federation of Chambers of Commerce (DIHT), Hans Peter Stihl, said he was optimistic about an end to the dispute, which has prompted mass protests in the metal and engineering sector and risks triggering all-out strikes next year.
"I am confident that we shall finally be able to move away from sick pay conditions in their current extreme form," Stihl was cited as saying in a newspaper interview.

Employers have offered to convert the cut in sick pay into a reduction in holiday entitlements based on a proportion of the time spent ill, but IG Metall has insisted that sick pay and related working conditions must remain in their present form.
